results.description:
Russia Africa Summit: 22 Presidents

The Russia Africa Summit 2026 closed in Moscow with 48 countries and 22 heads of state, up from 17 in 2023.  

Putin promised no "neo-colonial exploitation" and declared the era of a few states deciding "the fate of entire continents" over.

What he wanted:  Africa's 54 UN votes, military reach through the Africa Corps, minerals, and a trade system beyond sanctions.  Grain is Russia's main tool of influence: 13 million tonnes of farm products in the first nine months of 2026.  

The political return appeared in February 2026, when six African states voted against a UN peace resolution on Ukraine and 17 abstained.

What Africa wanted:  weapons, cheap grain, power plants, a bigger UN voice, and the freedom to deal with everyone.  Mali's leader, General Assimi Goïta, asked for "partnerships based on sovereignty, equality and non-interference."

Trade figures show that Russia is a much smaller partner.  

Trade with Africa in 2025:  Europe 385,000 million dollars, China 348,000 million dollars, the United States about 85,000 million dollars, Russia 27,000 million dollars.  

The United States total is less than half its trade with Vietnam alone.  Russia's real weight is the Africa Corps, about 2,000 men in the Sahel.

No leader mentioned the African recruits:  3,066 Africans lured into Russia's army with job offers, 502 confirmed dead.  Two days before the summit, a UN commission called it trafficking.

In the Sahel, the Africa Corps saved Niger's junta from a mutiny but cannot lift the jihadist fuel blockade on Bamako, the capital of Mali.  Egypt, an ally of the United States, is building a 25,000 million dollar nuclear plant with Russia.

The answer of the United States government is "commercial diplomacy" and minerals deals.  This is the right approach, but the Russian government brought together 22 presidents, and the United States has not.

Trade beats mercenaries.  The United States must be present in Africa, or other countries will take its place.

results.title: Unilateral sanctions don't work.
results.description:
Unilateral sanctions don't work. History proves that one-sided economic pressure fails to force a strategic retreat when a state views its security as a vital priority.

Look at what happened in the Sahel—years of U.S. sanctions targeting Mali's defense officials completely failed to change their strategy, ultimately forcing Washington to quietly lift them to salvage regional operations. Applying this pressure unevenly reveals a glaring double standard: penalizing Rwanda’s defense structures - which will not work - while giving the DRC preferential treatment, despite Kinshasa harboring extremist negative forces like the FDLR on its soil.

True stability requires balanced diplomacy and addressing all security threats, not blunt isolation.

results.title: Malian President Assimi Goïta at the 3rd Russia-Africa summit: "Partnership with the Sahel must be shaped around an approach based on listen
results.description:
Malian President Assimi Goïta at the 3rd Russia-Africa summit:

"Partnership with the Sahel must be shaped around an approach based on listening, mutual respect, trust, and the building of sustainable capacities. In this context, our partnership with the Russian Federation is a perfect example of what we expect. This is a sincere, win-win, respectful partnership that cares about the expectations of the population. Mali, within the framework of the Confederation of Sahel States, is in impartial cooperation with the Russian Federation and all sincere partners. It will continue its resolute and irreversible march towards the reconstruction of dignity and prosperity.
Together, let us work for the emergence of a more balanced, more stable, more solidaristic, multipolar world that respects the sovereignty of states for the prosperity of peoples. Long live the sincere and fruitful cooperation between Russia and Africa! Long live the historic friendship between Mali and Russia! Long live the Confederation of Sahel States! May God protect Mali and protect our people! Thank you."

Vladimir Putin:
"Dear colleague, you have spoken very truly, and everyone will agree with you in stating that the solution in the Sahel region is of great importance not only for Africa but for the entire world."

results.title: I didn't agree with her in the other clip that is going around but I do agree with this one.
results.description:
I didn't agree with her in the other clip that is going around but I do agree with this one.

The US played it too fast and loose with their ability to impose sanctions. Spit in allies faces by selling them weapons and weapons systems that only work when the US gives them permission to use them. Breaks treaties on a whim when it feels like. Abuses control of the swift system. Spent the last 65 years meddling in Latin American elections.

It's only natural that people are looking for ways to circumvent all that. I said a while back the goal for a BRICS currency almost certainly wouldnt be to challenge the dollars dominance. As long as the Euro been out it hasn't even come close. The goal is to be able to pay each other next time the US tries to  sanction one of them into bending the knee.

I see the increased prominence of coordination agreements like NB8, Mercosur, The Alliance of Sahel States etc to be the precursor to a multipolar world, polarized by region

results.title: Meanwhile, Africa is becoming increasingly crowded and eventful, including within the Africa Corps’ area of operations.
results.description:
Meanwhile, Africa is becoming increasingly crowded and eventful, including within the Africa Corps’ area of operations.

Algerian President Abdelmadjid Tebboune has decided to send army units into neighboring Niger. Algeria’s parliament approved the decision on October 25.

The stated purpose is “to protect the energy and economic interests shared by Algeria and Niger.”

Alongside Mali and Burkina Faso, Niger belongs to the Confederation of Sahel States, established on July 6, 2024, on the foundations of the Alliance of Sahel States. Like its fellow members, Niger is embroiled in prolonged fighting against various insurgent and terrorist organizations. An attempted military coup was also prevented in the summer of 2026.

The country is also within the Africa Corps’ area of operations. But with a territory covering 1.267 million square kilometers, there is no shortage of demand for troops. Many oil and gas export projects rely on Algeria as an export route and involve substantial Algerian participation, from financing to personnel. This has prompted Niger’s northern neighbor to take a direct role in protecting those projects.

results.title: PRESS RELEASE MINISTRY OF DEFENCE OCTOBER 29, 2026 NIGERIA ADVOCATES AFRICAN STRATEGIC AUTONOMY AND SOVEREIGN DEFENCE CAPABILITIES AS AFRIDE
results.description:
PRESS RELEASE

MINISTRY OF DEFENCE

OCTOBER 29, 2026

NIGERIA ADVOCATES AFRICAN STRATEGIC AUTONOMY AND SOVEREIGN DEFENCE CAPABILITIES AS AFRIDEX 2026 ENDS

LAGOS— The Honourable Minister of Defence, General Christopher Gwabin Musa (Rtd) OFR, has called for a decisive shift in Africa's approach to global security, urging African nations to transition from being a theatre of external geopolitical competition to becoming self-reliant, influential actors shaping global security decisions.
Delivering Nigeria’s resolve in a strategic engagement with visiting African Ministers of Defence and Chiefs of Defence Staff at the just concluded African Defence Exhibition and Conference (AFRIDEX 2026) in Lagos, the Honourable Minister reaffirmed Nigeria’s unwavering commitment to continental solidarity, collective security, and the rapid development of indigenous defence capabilities.
Emphasising the need for a unified continental posture, General Musa stated that growing global geopolitical competition and external interference make it imperative for Africa to champion a common position rooted in national sovereignty and strategic autonomy. Defence partnerships, the Minister noted, must henceforth align strictly with African-defined priorities rather than perpetuate strategic dependence or undermined state sovereignty.
The Minister highlighted the centrality of the African Union Peace and Security Architecture (AU-PSA) and called for stronger African representation in global security decision-making alongside greater coherence across continental, regional, and national defence frameworks.
Addressing the security climate across the Sahel, Lake Chad Basin, Horn of Africa, and parts of Central and Southern Africa, the Honourable Minister stressed that cross-border threats like terrorism, violent extremism, and organised crime cannot be solved through fragmented national responses. He therefore expressed Nigeria’s commitment to Cross-Regional Cooperation between ECOWAS member states and the Alliance of Sahel States (AES), Diplomatic & Peacebuilding Engagements to address protracted conflicts in Sudan and the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), as well as Integrated Governance Models to address the root causes of instability and promote civilian protection on the continent.
Highlighting Africa’s long-standing reliance on external military equipment, spare parts, and technical support as a key vulnerability, General Musa advocated for a bold transition toward local defence production, technology transfer, and joint maintenance ventures.
To effectively safeguard the continent, the Minister stressed the importance of turning the African Standby Force (ASF) into a fully operational, responsive, and strategically mobile capability with sustainable financing. Furthermore, he called for enhanced maritime domain awareness and coordinated naval exercises to protect strategic sea lines of communication in the Gulf of Guinea and the Red Sea.
The Honourable Minister proposed the creation of a structured follow-up mechanism among participating defence institutions to oversee joint training, intelligence fusion, and industrial joint ventures to ensure the discussions lead to measurable outcomes.
In conclusion, he said "Africa's security future must ultimately be determined by the collective resolve, capabilities, and strategic choices of African nations. Nigeria stands ready to work shoulder-to-shoulder with all partners toward a secure, united, and self-reliant continent."
The meeting congratulated Nigeria for putting together the first Defence Exhibition, committing to ensuring its sustainability for the attainment of security sovereignty.

SIGNED:
Leah Katung-Babatunde 
Special Assistant (Media) to the Honourable Minister of Defence Federal Republic of Nigeria

results.title: 🔘 The Moroccan Sahara at a Geostrategic Turning Point: The US–Russia Confrontation, MINURSO's Future and Morocco's Sovereignty Doctrine GEOP
results.description:
🔘  The Moroccan Sahara at a Geostrategic Turning Point: The US–Russia Confrontation, MINURSO's Future and Morocco's Sovereignty Doctrine

GEOPOLITICS | DIPLOMACY | INTERNATIONAL SECURITY | NORTH AFRICA

The developments surrounding the UN Security Council's deliberations on the Moroccan Sahara on 30 October 2026 represent a significant turning point in the diplomatic and geopolitical trajectory of the territorial dispute. The reported Russian veto against the American draft resolution, the failure of Moscow's alternative proposal, and the non-renewal of MINURSO's mandate have exposed profound divisions over the future international framework for addressing the issue.

Washington's initiative reflected an attempt to move beyond the traditional management of the dispute towards a more clearly defined political settlement based on Morocco's Autonomy Initiative. Strategically, the American approach sought to consolidate the growing international recognition of the autonomy proposal as a credible and realistic framework for negotiations.

Russia's opposition demonstrated the persistence of great-power competition within the Security Council. While Moscow exercised its veto power to prevent the adoption of the American proposal, it failed to secure sufficient support for its alternative. This diplomatic confrontation revealed the limits of Russia's capacity to shape the Council's collective position, despite its institutional power to block resolutions.

The Royal Cabinet's statement of 30 October introduced a particularly significant dimension. By interpreting the non-renewal of MINURSO's mandate as the beginning of a new political phase, Morocco signalled its determination to move beyond decades of repetitive UN conflict-management mechanisms.

From the perspective of Moroccan strategic doctrine, this development reinforces a sovereignty-centred approach grounded in territorial integrity, diplomatic continuity, regional stability and the consolidation of international partnerships.

The strategic significance also extends to Morocco's Atlantic and African ambitions. The Kingdom's southern provinces increasingly constitute a central component of its geoeconomic strategy, connecting Atlantic maritime infrastructure, African economic integration, energy corridors and regional connectivity.

Strategic Assessment

Three geopolitical implications deserve particular attention.

First, the American position strengthens Morocco's diplomatic leverage, even though the failure to adopt the draft prevents its proposed provisions from acquiring the authority of a new Security Council resolution.

Second, Russia's veto creates a new diplomatic challenge for Rabat, requiring a careful reassessment of relations with Moscow without necessarily undermining broader bilateral cooperation.

Third, the potential termination of MINURSO's operational mandate raises important questions concerning ceasefire monitoring, regional security and the future institutional role of the United Nations.

The non-renewal of a peacekeeping mandate does not, by itself, terminate the UN's involvement or resolve every legal dimension of the dispute.

Ultimately, the events of 30 October indicate a possible transition from prolonged international conflict management towards a more politically contested settlement process.

For Morocco, the strategic priority remains the consolidation of sovereignty, the strengthening of international support for its Autonomy Initiative, and the preservation of stability across the Sahara–Sahel and Atlantic geopolitical spaces.

The central strategic question is no longer limited to MINURSO's future, but concerns the balance of international influence that will determine the next phase of the Moroccan Sahara issue.

GEOSTRATEGIC INSIGHT
31 October 2026

results.title: The third "Russia-Africa" Summit is taking place in Moscow on October 28-29, 2026.
results.description:
The third "Russia-Africa" Summit is taking place in Moscow on October 28-29, 2026.

The main political outcome of the summit is that Moscow maintains extensive contacts with Africa despite the harm its policies inflict on Africans. According to the organizers, 48 countries confirmed their participation, with 22 of them represented by heads of state. At the previous summit in 2023, there were 17 such leaders, and at the first one in 2019, there were 43. This is a partial recovery in the level of participation, which the Kremlin can present as evidence of international recognition. A telling example is Kenya: last time it was represented by an ambassador, but now the delegation is led by President Ruto, although the issue of recruiting Kenyans into the Russian army remains acute.

A permanent cooperation framework consolidates Russian influence but does not guarantee that African partners will see promises fulfilled. On the sidelines of the summit, Lavrov and the Chairperson of the African Union Commission signed a plan for 2027-2029 covering 19 areas - from security to energy and education. This creates channels of work between summits and expands Moscow's access to African institutions. At the same time, the Russian Foreign Ministry admitted as early as June that previous meetings had produced more declarations than practical agreements.

Russian military support helps certain regimes stay in power and increases their dependence on Moscow. According to an FDD assessment, the geography of Russian military presence has expanded since 2023 to at least nine countries. Niger illustrates how such presence turns into political leverage. At the end of August, during a mutiny by part of the military, Russian forces helped the authorities suppress the uprising. According to the Russian ambassador, the Nigerien side itself requested the assistance.

Dependence on Russian support can persist even when it fails to provide reliable security and is accompanied by violence against the population. In the spring the Africa Corps was forced to leave Kidal in northern Mali. In October, Malian forces with Russian support retook the city, yet the episode demonstrated the limits of Moscow's capabilities. Konrad-Adenauer-Stiftung expert Ulf Laessing explains the preservation of the partnership by the lack of viable alternatives for the Malian authorities. Meanwhile, in October, Human Rights Watch documented new instances of torture against civilians involving Russian mercenaries from the Africa Corps.

Russia is increasing its revenues from food supplies to Africa even as its own actions contribute to food insecurity. In the first nine months of 2026 Moscow delivered more than $3.7 billion worth of agricultural products to Africa - 9% more than a year earlier. The largest increase in monetary terms came from Kenya, which is simultaneously pressing for a resolution of the problem of its citizens in the Russian army. Food supplies have value for buyers, but they must be assessed alongside the consequences of Russia's war against Ukraine. After Russia's withdrawal from the Black Sea Grain Initiative in 2023, the UN Secretary-General warned of the impact on vulnerable countries and of rising prices.

Nuclear energy risks turning the need for electricity into long-term dependence on Russia. Rosatom presented floating nuclear power plants and reported advanced negotiations with Egypt, Togo, Namibia and Tanzania. The proposed model involves the purchase of electricity while retaining Russian involvement in maintenance and fuel supply. The plants can operate for up to 60 years, making the link with the supplier long-lasting and difficult to replace. There are still no publicly confirmed contracts for these projects, agreed financing or schedules. The largest project already under way is the construction of the El Dabaa nuclear power plant in Egypt.
Opaque links between Russian payment networks create financial and sanctions risks for African partners. Putin called for expanding ties between banks, opening branches and using Russia's SPFS alongside the pan-African payment system. In this way Moscow seeks to connect its own instruments with African infrastructure.

A separate track is the A7 cryptocurrency network: in April the Financial Times wrote of limited evidence of its practical progress on the continent, but in October the Centre for Information Resilience identified numerous technical links with international payment platforms, including the Togo-linked Amani AI. Participants in the A7 network are under British sanctions.

Russian expansion in the gold-mining sector can weaken state control over national resources and channel revenues towards Russian military objectives. This mechanism is already visible in the Central African Republic: according to the US Treasury, the Wagner-linked company Midas, together with mercenaries, obstructed state inspections of the Ndassima mine, while revenues of related companies supported military operations. Against this background, new projects require particular attention. In Mali a gold-processing plant is under construction: 62% of the joint company belongs to the state, 38% to the Russian firm Yadran. Processing of raw materials from other Sahel countries is being considered, which could turn the plant into a regional hub. In Niger, Rosgeologia has so far reported only readiness to sign agreements on hydrocarbon and gold exploration. For Moscow, gold is valuable both as income and as an asset for operations outside ordinary Western banking channels.

Russia's media presence combines open agreements with covert operations that mislead African audiences. Ahead of the summit, TASS signed agreements with media partners in Burundi, Guinea, Cameroon, Mali, Niger, the Seychelles and Tanzania on news exchange, training and reciprocal visits. The network covers both close security partners of Moscow and states with other forms of cooperation. According to RT, TASS also provides its news feeds free of charge to more than 300 African media outlets. This work began long before the current summit and ensures continuous access to newsrooms. In parallel, Graphika and Code for Africa identified a network of likely fabricated journalists and experts promoting Russian interests; researchers have a high level of confidence regarding 38 such individuals.

The recruitment of Africans for the war is a direct human cost that is not offset by trade or diplomatic benefits. In August the Ukrainian Foreign Ministry reported at least 2 982 recruits from 37 African countries and around 486 known deaths. These are incomplete figures from the Ukrainian side, but independent research confirms the mechanism of abuse. Amnesty International has documented deception, coercion and the exploitation of economic hardship that in many cases amount to human trafficking. In Kenya, families are publicly demanding answers and the return of their relatives.

Russian military presence draws African states into Moscow's broader struggle for strategic positions. Russia has long sought a permanent naval presence on the continent, but this remains an unrealized ambition. The project in Port Sudan has been delayed for years. As late as the end of 2025 the Russian ambassador explained the pause by the war; Sudan Tribune, citing its own sources at the time, reported that al-Burhan had assured the Saudi side that plans for a Red Sea base had been frozen. At the same time Russia is expanding access to Libyan airfields, including Maaten al-Sarra near the borders with Chad and Sudan, supporting its operations in the Sahel. The infrastructure already exists, although guaranteed long-term access and a permanent naval base remain unresolved. The harm from previous operations in Libya is concrete: Human Rights Watch established Wagner's involvement in the mining of areas near Tripoli in 2020.

The gap between the Russian offer and the development needs of African countries risks perpetuating their economic vulnerability. The co-chair of the summit, President of Burundi Évariste Ndayishimiye, called on Russian companies to invest in local processing, jobs and skills transfer. For African governments it is important to retain a larger share of the revenues from their own resources. This is precisely where the Russian offer falls short: trade (with a surplus in Russia's favor) is more developed than large-scale productive investment.
Without the development of local production and skills, countries can remain suppliers of raw materials and buyers of finished goods. This suits Moscow but does not help its partners in Africa.

The principal danger of the Russian model is the transformation of vital needs of African societies into dependence, a significant share of whose costs is borne by the African population itself. Moscow entrenches itself through military support, food supplies and, in prospect, electricity. In the three years between summits it has expanded its presence and strengthened ties with a number of African states, gaining influence without large-scale investment in development. The social cost of this model of cooperation can already be assessed: violence against civilians, recruitment by deception, covert information operations and the restriction of state control over resources have all been documented.

The third "Russia-Africa" Summit is taking place in Moscow on October 28-29, 2026.

The main political outcome of the summit is that Moscow maintains extensive contacts with Africa despite the harm its policies inflict on Africans. According to the organizers, 48 countries confirmed their participation, with 22 of them represented by heads of state. At the previous summit in 2023, there were 17 such leaders, and at the first one in 2019, there were 43. This is a partial recovery in the level of participation, which the Kremlin can present as evidence of international recognition. A telling example is Kenya: last time it was represented by an ambassador, but now the delegation is led by President Ruto, although the issue of recruiting Kenyans into the Russian army remains acute.

A permanent cooperation framework consolidates Russian influence but does not guarantee that African partners will see promises fulfilled. On the sidelines of the summit, Lavrov and the Chairperson of the African Union Commission signed a plan for 2027-2029 covering 19 areas - from security to energy and education. This creates channels of work between summits and expands Moscow's access to African institutions. At the same time, the Russian Foreign Ministry admitted as early as June that previous meetings had produced more declarations than practical agreements.

Russian military support helps certain regimes stay in power and increases their dependence on Moscow. According to an FDD assessment, the geography of Russian military presence has expanded since 2023 to at least nine countries. Niger illustrates how such presence turns into political leverage. At the end of August, during a mutiny by part of the military, Russian forces helped the authorities suppress the uprising. According to the Russian ambassador, the Nigerien side itself requested the assistance.

Dependence on Russian support can persist even when it fails to provide reliable security and is accompanied by violence against the population. In the spring the Africa Corps was forced to leave Kidal in northern Mali. In October, Malian forces with Russian support retook the city, yet the episode demonstrated the limits of Moscow's capabilities. Konrad-Adenauer-Stiftung expert Ulf Laessing explains the preservation of the partnership by the lack of viable alternatives for the Malian authorities. Meanwhile, in October, Human Rights Watch documented new instances of torture against civilians involving Russian mercenaries from the Africa Corps.

results.description:
#RadioMoskva

3rd Africa Russian summit

Putin is having fun as delegations from 48 of Africa's 54 countries, 22 led by heads of state, are in Moscow for the third Russia-Africa summit, where Putin is selling Russia as Africa's anti-colonial partner.

He is on a roll to an eager audience, giving rousing speeches on his favourite topic: the world has been ruled by a bunch of neo-colonist imperialists that are just interested in bleeding the developing world of its human capital wealth to enrich themselves and the workers of the Global South should unite!

This is the third time for the summit, following the first one in Sochi in 2019 and it has been a huge success. The message resonates as much of the message is true. A study we reported found that the West exports some 80% of its manufacturing needs to the developing world, to sweat shops in places like Myanmar, where the “multinationals” pay pennies to have our phones and jeans made. That really does export the human capital wealth from these countries and enrich us in the developed world as a iPhone costs $1,000 and not the $5,000 it would cost if an American made it. That’s $4,000 of cash you can spend on something else. This system was politely known as “globalization” until recently but, as Putin keeps pushing, it can also be called neo-colonialism. At least, the Africans see it that way.

Ironically, this system is exactly what US President Donald Trump is complaining about and the reason for his Liberation Day tariffs – to bring “good manufacturing jobs back home.”

But this is beyond stupid, as it takes no account of the income delta: we did a back of the envelope calculation of the unit cost of making a widget in the EU, US and China using one kilo of metal, 100kWh of power and an hour of average labour: it costs around $25 in the developed world and only $7 in China – and China already has some of the more expensive labour costs in the EMs.

You can’t compete with this, no matter how high you build your trade protectionist walls. As we have been arguing all year, we are now in a post-Pax Americana world as the “emerging markets” have emerged. They should be renamed something like the “dynamic markets” (that is not really catchy enough, eh?) as they still have a lot of problems and the wage delta remains, but the China story shows very clearly that they are catching up in a lot of sectors and even overtaking the DMs in things like Greentech.

But not Africa. That really is still an emerging market story. The per capita incomes in Africa are still a fraction of even Russia’s income. It’s the last really big EM catch up story that has yet to unwind. And Russia is promising to help.

Russia was in the first wave. I was in the room at Putin’s first ever state of the nation speech in 2000 when he put demographics at the top of the agenda – it’s still top of the list – but he his top economic agenda item was to “catch up with Portugal.”

26 years later Russia has overtaken not only Portugal, but everyone else, except the US on a ppp basis.

This process is going in waves. Central Europe caught up with the DMs really fast after the EU accession wave in 2003. China has seen its growth accelerate for about a decade and is now slowing and maturing. Central Asia is only coming to its critical mass now, where Uzbekistan has been putting in 6% growth for a decade but recently started to accelerate and growth is now around 8% with another decade of fast growth ahead. Latin America is doing the same and the Brazilian economy in particular has been transformed and now accounts for a third of GDP of the whole continent by itself.

Africa is right at the start of the process, with a few hot spots like Nigeria. Sub-Saharan African growth averaged 4.5% in both 2026 and 2027 with East Africa growing the fastest at 6.5% projected for this year.

It usually starts with FDI into light manufacturing, but most of Africa is still at the exporting-raw-materials stage. It’s an issue of low wages vs productivity. The Balkans is currently booming as productivity has risen to the point where the combination of the two makes it more profitable than investing in Central Europe. In Africa the wages are essentially zero, but so is the productivity.

In this context, listening to Putin’s speeches today and yesterday and he is pushing all of Africa’s buttons. He is not only promising to provide grain – a top necessity for many countries – but yesterday he also promised to invest into African pharmaceutical sector, and today promised to build factories and move some Russian production to Africa. He also mentioned that the number of African students studying in Russia has doubled in the last year and Rosatom was holding talks on building half a dozen floating nuclear power stations in Africa. These are all productivity multipliers and the assembled presidents are creaming themselves over the prospects as Russia usually finances these sorts of investments itself – for the Africans they are essentially free (in the short-term but come with strategic dependencies…).

The neo-colonial troupe is the Xmas wrapping paper this is all bundled into. Another story earlier this month that went by largely unnoticed was a Russia sponsored UN motion to condemn sanctions as neo-colonial, which was universally approved by the Global South and university condemned by the EU and US. The Kremlin completely outplayed the West with that one. France was booted out of Niger in 2023 because it was paying a fraction for a kilo for uranium, an estimated €68/kg, when the market price was closer to €200. Macron regularly gets booed when he tours in francophone Africa – he simply doesn’t get it.

All this is important as its part of Putin’s big bet on the Global South Century. He must have been fully aware of what would happen when he marched into Ukraine – a permeant break with the West and the end of his dream of a single market “from Lisbon to Vladivostok” which most of his foreign policy was built around. Swapping Germany for Sahel may not look like such a great idea, but when you add in Latam, SE Asia and particularly China, it starts to get more appealing: Putin pointed out that just the BRICS generated 40% of global GDP last year. And Africa will eventually be a big catch as it shares many features with Russia: a large land mass, a large population, and a cornucopia of raw materials. Putin’s plan is clearly to accelerate the catch up, and the Africans are lovin’ it.

Russia is so well received as it never tried to colonise Africa and indeed, during the Cold War the communist USSR supported the independence movements against their colonial overlords. And since then Russia remains the destination of choice for a quality higher education. You’d be surprised at how many of the African delegates in Moscow today speak fluent Russian from their university days. For example, presidents João Lourenço of Angola and John Dramani Mahama of Ghana both studied in Moscow.
